title: The Sharpe Pint

opening_mood.text: Morning all. Grab a coffee, or if you are reading this on Friday afternoon, start eyeing up the nearest pint of bitter. We have got a packed slate today: private equity trying to pull off one of the biggest software buyouts in history, AI investors losing their minds over a potential $2 trillion IPO, Elon Musk buying his way out of a three-year Scandinavian standoff, and the Rhine running so dry that German steelmakers are practically pushing their own barges. Let us get into it.

content.text: 1. Anthropic's Backers Eye a $2 Trillion October IPO

What happened: Investors in Claude-maker Anthropic are reportedly targeting a valuation of $2 trillion or more for its planned October IPO. This would make it the largest stock-market debut in history, eclipsing SpaceX's record listing. The valuation is driven by expectations of annualised revenue reaching $100B-$120B by December 2026 (up from $47B in May).

Why it matters: It is the ultimate litmus test for the AI trade. While sceptics point to negative cash flows and the lack of a public peer, bulls argue that 800% annual growth justifies a 30x or higher revenue multiple (especially when Palantir trades near 55x).

The City angle: For asset managers and equity research analysts, this is the moment of truth. Private valuations have been marked up aggressively in secondary markets. If public markets reject a $2tn valuation, it could trigger a massive repricing across the entire AI infrastructure stack.

What to say: 'The $2 trillion target is classic venture capitalist wishcasting, but if they actually hit $100 billion in annualised revenue by December, a 20x multiple does not look completely insane compared to Palantir trading at over 50x. The real question is whether that revenue is durable or just a temporary land grab while everyone builds their initial LLM stacks.'
2. Silver Lake Eyes $50bn-Plus Take-Private of Workday

What happened: Private equity giant Silver Lake is in preliminary talks to acquire HR and financial software provider Workday in a deal that could value it at over $50 billion. Workday's shares jumped nearly 18% on Thursday following the Reuters report, lifting its market cap to $51.1 billion.

Why it matters: This would rank among the largest software buyouts in history. It is also a fascinating signal that private equity is ready to hunt for marquee SaaS names that have been beaten down by public market fears that AI will disrupt their per-seat subscription models.

The City angle: For investment bankers, this is a sign that mega-LBOs are back. Silver Lake is reportedly looking to bring in co-investors (having previously partnered with Saudi's PIF on the $55bn EA take-private). It also shows that PE sees massive, stable cash flows in 'boring' back-office software that public markets are underestimating.

What to say: 'Silver Lake's move on Workday is a classic PE play: buying highly defensive, recurring cash flows when the public market gets jittery about AI disruption. If they can pull this off at over $50 billion, it proves that the mega-LBO market isn't dead, it's just waiting for the right SaaS cash cow.'
3. Tesla Defeats Sweden's IF Metall in Historic 1,021-Day Strike

What happened: Swedish trade union IF Metall has called off its historic 1,021-day strike against Tesla after the carmaker systematically 'bought out' all remaining striking union members at the company, rendering the industrial action ineffective.

Why it matters: This is a massive victory for Elon Musk's anti-union stance and a major blow to the 'Nordic model' of collective bargaining. Despite sympathy strikes from dockworkers, postal workers, and neighbouring countries, Tesla managed to route around the blockades and ultimately paid its way out of the conflict.

The City angle: For ESG-focused asset managers, this is a complicated one. On one hand, it shows Tesla's operational resilience and ability to protect its margins against labour pressure. On the other, it highlights the governance and social risks of investing in a company that is willing to break traditional labour norms in key European markets.

What to say: 'Tesla essentially used its massive balance sheet to buy out the strikers and break the longest strike in modern Swedish history. It is a brutal reminder that in a war of attrition between a trillion-dollar multinational and a local union, cash is king—even in Scandinavia.'
4. The Rhine Runs Dry, Forcing Thyssenkrupp to Cut Output

What happened: Water levels on the Rhine River have hit historic lows, with the critical chokepoint at Kaub dropping to record depths. This has severely disrupted shipping on Europe's key trade artery, forcing industrial giant Thyssenkrupp to reduce steel output at its Duisburg plant due to raw material supply constraints.

Why it matters: The Rhine handles around 80% of Germany's inland waterway traffic. When water levels drop, barges must carry lighter loads or stop entirely, driving freight rates to record highs and forcing companies to switch to expensive road or rail alternatives.

The City angle: For macro traders and European equity analysts, this is a supply-chain headache that acts as a drag on Germany's already struggling industrial economy. It also highlights the growing 'climate risk' premium that investors must price into European heavy industry.

What to say: 'Thyssenkrupp cutting output because the Rhine is dry shows how vulnerable European heavy industry is to infrastructure bottlenecks. When your primary shipping route turns into a sandbank, switching to rail and road isn't just expensive—it's logistically painful when the German rail network is already stretched.'
5. US 10-Year Treasury Auction Clears at Highest Yield Since 2007

What happened: The U.S. Treasury's $42 billion auction of 10-year notes cleared at a high yield of 4.683%, the highest since the 2007 global financial crisis. Despite the high yield, demand was strong, with indirect bidders (including foreign central banks) taking 76.7% of the offering.

Why it matters: The auction cleared almost exactly in line with pre-sale expectations, indicating that global investors are highly receptive to locking in yields at these elevated levels. It also eased fears that the massive supply of U.S. debt would struggle to find buyers.

The City angle: For fixed-income desks and macro hedge funds, this is a constructive signal. It shows that despite swelling U.S. budget deficits, global appetite for the world's risk-free asset remains robust. It also sets a solid foundation for the broader credit markets.

What to say: 'Clearing a 10-year auction at 4.68% with almost no tail and 76% indirect bidding shows that global investors are still hungry for U.S. duration at these yields. It suggests that even with massive supply, the bond vigilantes aren't quite ready to strike as long as the yields are this juicy.'
6. Parker-Hannifin Closes $9.25 Billion Acquisition of Filtration Group

What happened: Fortune 250 industrial leader Parker-Hannifin completed its massive $9.25 billion cash-free, debt-free acquisition of Filtration Group Corporation. To finance the deal, the company borrowed $7.75 billion under two separate credit facilities.

Why it matters: This is one of the largest deals in Parker-Hannifin's history and is a major play for high-margin, recurring aftermarket revenue. Filtration Group gets about 85% of its sales from recurring aftermarket products, which provides highly stable cash flows.

The City angle: For industrial equity analysts, this is a textbook portfolio transformation. Parker-Hannifin is shifting away from cyclical OEM sales toward steady, high-margin aftermarket consumables. The market typically rewards this shift with higher valuation multiples.

What to say: 'Parker-Hannifin borrowing $7.75 billion to close the Filtration Group deal is a massive bet on recurring aftermarket revenue. In a choppy macro environment, owning a business where 85% of sales are high-margin replacement filters that customers have to buy is exactly the kind of defensive moat the market will pay up for.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Big Picture: S&P 7,800 and the Great Inflation Cool-Off

If you spent Thursday watching the screens, you would be forgiven for thinking the Federal Reserve has finally managed to orchestrate the mythical 'soft landing' without scraping the paintwork. The S&P 500 climbed 0.65% to close at 7,798.99, having briefly popped its head above the 7,800 milestone for the first time in intraday trading. The Nasdaq Composite led the charge, up 0.81% to 26,803.03, while the Dow Jones squeaked out a 0.13% gain to 53,839.99. The catalyst? A double-whammy of cooling inflation data that has traders breathing a massive sigh of relief.
Why the Fed is Breathing Easier

Hot on the heels of Wednesday's in-line CPI print, which saw annual inflation ease to 3.4%, Thursday's Producer Price Index (PPI) came in flatter than a pint of lager left out overnight. Headline monthly PPI was dead flat (0.0% vs 0.1% expected), and core PPI rose just 0.2%. For the macro desks, this is the pipeline relief they have been praying for. The immediate cross-asset read was clear: the probability of a September Fed rate hike plummeted from over 55% last week to under 35%. Treasury yields took the hint, with the 10-year easing to 4.65% and the policy-sensitive 2-year slipping to 4.18%.
Crude Reality: Oil Slips on Demand Fears

It was not just inflation data giving equities a leg up; a sharp drop in energy costs did some of the heavy lifting. Brent crude tumbled 2.1% to $87.30 a barrel, snapping a six-day rally. While geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and the blockaded Strait of Hormuz are still keeping risk managers awake, the physical market is telling a different story. OPEC trimmed its 2026 global demand growth forecast, and US commercial crude inventories just posted their largest weekly build since early 2023. Cheaper fuel is a massive boon for consumer cyclicals and airlines, but as we will see, it was not such good news for the home crowd.
The London Discount: FTSE 100 Drags Its Feet

While Wall Street was popping champagne, the Square Mile was nursing a mild hangover. The FTSE 100 fell 0.56% to close at 10,772.67, marking its fourth consecutive day of losses. This underperformance came despite some genuinely decent domestic news: UK GDP unexpectedly grew by 0.3% in June, putting Britain on track for the strongest first-half growth in the G7. So why the long faces?

items: The Commodity Curse: The FTSE is notoriously heavy on miners and oil majors, and Thursday was a perfect storm for both. Antofagasta plunged 6.8% after slashing its full-year copper production guidance due to a weather-related shutdown at its Los Pelambres mine in Chile. This dragged down peers like Rio Tinto (-4.1%) and Anglo American (-3.0%).
Oil Slick: With Brent crude sliding over 2%, index heavyweights BP (-1.9%) and Shell (-1.2%) acted as massive anchors on the blue-chip index.
The Divergence: While the DAX managed a 0.6% gain, London's commodity-heavy mix meant it completely missed out on the global risk-on party.

content.text: AI and Corporate Movers: Silver Lake and the Hardware Reality Check

In corporate land, the AI narrative continues to bifurcate. Software is still king: Workday skyrocketed 18% on reports that private equity giant Silver Lake is sniffing around for a buyout. Meanwhile, in Asia, South Korea's Kospi jumped 3.6%, propelled by AI memory giants Samsung and SK Hynix. But if you look at the physical hardware layer, the cracks are showing. Cerebras Systems crashed 17% after reporting a decline in hardware revenue, and Cisco's shares dipped after a disappointing outlook overshadowed an earnings beat. The lesson for analysts? The market is starting to demand actual revenue conversion from the massive capex boom, rather than just buying the AI hype.
Gold and Crypto: Taking a Breather

Elsewhere, gold eased back 0.6% to $4,379.41 an ounce. Do not weep for the gold bugs, though; the yellow metal has had a spectacular August, surging from sub-$4,000 levels in July as real yields compressed. Thursday's minor pullback looks like classic profit-taking rather than a change in trend. Bitcoin remained relatively sedate, hovering around the $63,650 mark, seemingly content to let the macro dust settle.
The Pub Discussion Point

Next time you are standing at the bar, here is the contrarian take to throw out: Is the market celebrating too early on the Fed hold? Yes, the monthly inflation prints are cooling, but annual PPI is still running at 4.7% and the US national debt has quietly crossed the $40 trillion mark. With the latest 10-year Treasury auction clearing at yields not seen since the financial crisis, the long end of the curve is still screaming that fiscal deficits and term premiums are not going away. The Fed might be able to sit on its hands in September, but the bond vigilantes are still very much awake.

content.text: Active Share: Exposing the Closet Indexers

Imagine walking into a pub, ordering a craft pint of some obscure, triple-hopped, artisanal IPA, paying eight pounds fifty for the privilege, and watching the bartender pour eighty percent cheap supermarket lager into the glass before topping it up with a splash of the good stuff. You would be livid. Yet, in the asset management world, millions of investors do exactly this every single day. They pay active management fees (often one percent to one point five percent of assets under management) to managers who do nothing more than hug their benchmark index. This is known as closet indexing, and the tool we use to expose it is called Active Share.

Introduced in 2009 by Yale academics Martijn Cremers and Antti Petajisto, Active Share is a beautifully simple metric. It measures the percentage of an investment portfolio’s holdings that differ from its benchmark index. If a fund has an Active Share of zero percent, it is a perfect carbon copy of the index (a tracker). If it has an Active Share of one hundred percent, it shares absolutely zero overlap with the benchmark. Generally, anything below sixty percent is considered a closet indexer, while anything above eighty percent is a genuinely active, high-conviction fund.
The Math: How to Calculate It
There are two ways to calculate Active Share, but the easiest way to think about it is one hundred percent minus the overlap.
Active Share = 100% - Sum of [ Minimum(Fund Weight_i, Benchmark Weight_i) ]

Let us look at a simple three-stock universe to see how this works in practice. Suppose the benchmark index consists of Stock A at fifty percent, Stock B at thirty percent, and Stock C at twenty percent. An active manager comes along and builds a portfolio with Stock A at forty percent, Stock B at forty percent, Stock C at zero percent, and Stock D (a stock not even in the benchmark) at twenty percent.

To find the Active Share, we first look at the overlap for each stock (the minimum weight in both): Stock A is forty percent, Stock B is thirty percent, Stock C is zero percent, and Stock D is zero percent. Summing these up, the total overlap is seventy percent. Therefore, the Active Share is thirty percent. Despite the manager claiming they are active and picking a completely off-benchmark stock, seventy percent of their portfolio is just replicating the index.
Why It Matters: The Active Fee Trap

Why should anyone in finance care? Because of the economics of active fees. If a fund charges a one percent management fee and has an Active Share of only twenty-five percent, the manager is only actively managing a quarter of your money. The other seventy-five percent is just tracking the index—something you could buy via a passive ETF for about five basis points.
If you calculate the implied active fee (the fee charged on the portion of the portfolio that is actually active), the numbers get terrifying. In this case, the formula is:
Implied Active Fee = [ Total Fee - (Passive Fee * (1 - Active Share)) ] / Active Share

Plugging in our numbers: [ 1.0% - (0.05% * 0.75) ] / 0.25 = 3.85%. You are effectively paying a hedge-fund-like three point eighty-five percent fee for the active portion of that portfolio. It is mathematically almost impossible for a manager to generate enough alpha to overcome that kind of cost drag.
Active Share vs. Tracking Error

A common point of confusion is how Active Share differs from Tracking Error. Active Share is a holdings-based metric. It does not care about volatility, correlations, or market conditions; it just looks at the weights. Tracking Error is a returns-based metric. It measures the standard deviation of the excess returns of the fund relative to the benchmark.

This creates a classic two-by-two matrix that every allocator uses. High Active Share and High Tracking Error represents the classic concentrated stock-picker. High Active Share and Low Tracking Error represents a diversified stock-picker who holds many off-benchmark stocks but manages sector and factor exposures so tightly that the overall returns behave like the index. Low Active Share and Low Tracking Error is your classic closet indexer. Finally, Low Active Share and High Tracking Error is a fund that holds index stocks but uses leverage, derivatives, or extreme sector timing bets.
Common Beginner Mistake: Equating Active Share with Skill

The biggest mistake people make is assuming that a high Active Share guarantees outperformance. It does not. Active Share is a measure of activity, not skill. You can have a one hundred percent Active Share fund that simply buys the twenty worst-performing stocks in the market. High Active Share is a necessary condition for generating significant alpha, but it is not a sufficient one. It simply increases the dispersion of outcomes, giving the manager the rope to either climb to glory or hang themselves.
How to Use This in Interviews and at Work

If you are interviewing at an active equity asset manager, this is a golden topic. Do not just ask about their investment process. Instead, ask: 'How do you balance your Active Share target with your Tracking Error budget? Do you find that clients are willing to tolerate the short-term underperformance that inevitably comes with a high Active Share?' This shows you understand portfolio construction, client psychology, and the commercial realities of running a fund.

If you are talking to colleagues or clients, you can use Active Share to critique the trend of multi-manager portfolios. When a pension fund hires five different high-conviction managers, their individual portfolios often overlap in a way that washes out. At the aggregate pension fund level, the Active Share collapses to thirty percent, but the client is still paying active fees to all five managers. It is a classic portfolio construction trap known as overlap drag.

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Death of the Two-Step: Jointly Learning Factors and Trading Policies

Traditional statistical arbitrage is a bit of a shotgun marriage. First, you build a risk factor model (like PCA or IPCA) to strip out systematic market beta and isolate the "idiosyncratic" residuals. Second, you hand those residuals over to a sequence model (like an LSTM or a transformer) to find mean-reverting trading signals. The problem? Your factor model doesn't know or care about your trading strategy. It is optimised to explain total market variance. Consequently, the residuals it spits out are often highly illiquid, expensive to short, or require massive, high-turnover rebalancing. By the time your execution desk is finished, your beautiful backtested Sharpe ratio has been thoroughly chewed up by transaction costs.
Enter Attention Factors

A recent paper presented at the International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2025) by researchers at Stanford and Hanwha Life introduces an elegant solution: the Attention Factor Model. Instead of a disjointed two-step process, they propose a one-step end-to-end framework that jointly learns the risk factors, identifies the mispricing, and optimises the trading weights.

The model uses an attention mechanism on firm characteristics (like momentum, valuation, and size) to construct time-varying factor loadings. It then feeds the resulting residuals into a sequence model to generate trading signals. Crucially, the entire pipeline is trained together, with the loss function directly optimising the net Sharpe ratio (after transaction costs) rather than generic mean squared error.
Why "Weak" Factors are Goldmines

One of the most fascinating insights from the paper is the role of "weak" factors. In traditional PCA, you throw away factors with low eigenvalues because they don't explain much market-wide variance. But the authors show that these weak factors are actually crucial for statistical arbitrage. They capture the subtle, localised boundaries of asset similarity (e.g., specific sub-industries or niche thematic groups) where temporary price discrepancies occur. By training the factor model and the trading policy jointly, the network deliberately seeks out and preserves these weak factors because they are highly profitable to trade, while ignoring high-variance factors that are too expensive to exploit.
PyTorch Concept: Joint Factor & Net Sharpe Optimisation

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class AttentionFactorStatArb(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_chars, num_factors, num_assets):
        super().__init__()
        self.queries = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(num_factors, num_chars))
        self.char_proj = nn.Linear(num_chars, num_chars)
        self.signal_net = nn.Linear(num_assets, num_assets)

    def forward(self, R, X, prev_W, tc_coeff=0.001):
        proj_X = self.char_proj(X)
        Beta = torch.softmax(torch.matmul(proj_X, self.queries.T) / (X.shape[-1]**0.5), dim=0)
        F = torch.matmul(Beta.T, R)
        Epsilon = R - torch.matmul(Beta, F)
        W = torch.softmax(self.signal_net(Epsilon), dim=0)
        net_return = torch.sum(W * R) - tc_coeff * torch.sum(torch.abs(W - prev_W))
        return net_return, W
The Pub/Interview Talking Point

If you are interviewing for a quant role or chatting with your systematic PM, this is a killer concept to bring up. The standard industry line is: "We run PCA to get our residuals, and then we trade them." You can counter with: "But PCA is blind to transaction costs and trading objectives. If you don't estimate your factor model and your trading policy jointly, you're likely wasting capital on high-turnover 'phantom alpha' in illiquid residuals. Plus, standard PCA throws away the weak factors, which are exactly where the most profitable, localised mispricings live."
The Catch

Before you go and deploy this on your personal account, there is a massive practical hurdle: data alignment. To train this model, you need a high-quality, point-in-time dataset of dozens of firm characteristics (like the Open Source Asset Pricing dataset) mapped perfectly to historical price data. In the academic paper, they use CRSP PERMNOs. If you don't have an institutional subscription to CRSP/Compustat, mapping these identifiers to standard tickers without survivorship or lookahead bias is an absolute nightmare. Furthermore, end-to-end Sharpe optimisation is notoriously sensitive; if your transaction cost model is even slightly too optimistic, the neural net will immediately find a way to exploit that loophole, leaving you with a model that looks like a money-printer in backtests but bleeds cash in production.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Myth of the Smart Crowd

We have all heard the pitch for decentralized prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi. The narrative is beautiful, almost democratic: by giving thousands of people "skin in the game", the collective "wisdom of the crowd" aggregates disparate information into an incredibly accurate forecasting machine. It is a great story, especially for the platforms themselves. But a brilliant paper by researchers at the London Business School and Yale completely dismantles it. It turns out prediction markets are not accurate because the crowd is smart. They are accurate because a tiny, hyper-disciplined elite is systematically skinning everyone else.
The Paper

The paper is titled "Prediction Market Accuracy: Crowd Wisdom or Informed Minority?" (SSRN Working Paper No. 6617059) by Roberto Gomez-Cram, Yunhan Guo, Howard Kung (all LBS), and Theis Ingerslev Jensen (Yale). The authors did not just skim the surface; they analysed the entire transaction history of Polymarket from 2023 to 2025. We are talking about 1.72 million accounts, over 210,000 individual markets, and a massive $13.76 billion in trading volume. To separate genuine skill from pure luck, they ran 10,000 randomized simulations for every single trader. The results are a cold shower for retail punters.
The Key Takeaways

items: The 3% Rule: Only 3.14% of accounts qualify as "skilled winners"—traders whose positions consistently and accurately predict both short-term price trends and final outcomes.
The Wealth Transfer: Together with market makers, this tiny 3% elite captures more than 30% of all profits on the platform.

The Food Chain: Meanwhile, roughly 67% of accounts are net losers. Their trades generate plenty of volume but zero useful information. In the authors' words, their losses "flow as profits to the informed minority".

Scary Persistence: Unlike traditional active mutual funds, where only about 10% of "skilled" managers retain their edge out-of-sample, a whopping 44% of Polymarket's skilled traders maintained their elite status in out-of-sample testing.

No Insiders Required: While they did spot a tiny group of potential insiders (about 1,950 accounts opening right before specific events), the bulk of the market's accuracy comes from this skilled minority reacting instantly to public news and correcting the crowd's behavioural mistakes.

content.text: The Killer Quote
"Prediction market accuracy thus reflects the wisdom of an informed minority, not the wisdom of the crowd."
How to Read It

If you want to read the paper, focus on the introduction and the empirical results sections. You can safely skim the heavy econometric modelling and the mathematical formulation of the sign-randomization tests unless you are a quant looking to replicate their methodology. Focus on the charts showing the distribution of trader returns and the out-of-sample persistence metrics.
Why It Matters to You

If you work in asset management, macro research, or investment banking, you probably monitor prediction markets as a real-time sentiment gauge for elections, central bank decisions, or corporate events. This paper gives you a massive confidence boost in those signals: they are highly accurate because they are being policed by sharp, fast-reacting arbitrageurs. However, if you are casually betting on these platforms over your weekend pint, this is a stark warning. Unless you have a proprietary data feed, a custom LLM scraper, and a disciplined risk model, you are not part of the "wise crowd"—you are the liquidity feeding the sharks.
The Sharpe Pint Take

This paper confirms what anyone who has ever sat on a trading desk already knows: markets are not democracies. The "wisdom of crowds" is a marketing slogan designed to make retail investors feel clever while they get systematically harvested. But there is a beautiful irony here. The very fact that these platforms are flooded with retail "dumb money" is what attracts the sophisticated quants and arbitrageurs who make the prices accurate in the first place. If you are using these markets for macro signals, trust the price—the sharks are doing their job. Just do not mistake yourself for one of them.
What to Say at the Pub

items: "Did you see that LBS and Yale paper on Polymarket? It completely busts the 'wisdom of crowds' myth. Only 3% of traders drive the accuracy, while two-thirds of accounts just bleed cash to them."

"It is wild that prediction market edge is so persistent—44% out-of-sample compared to just 10% for active mutual fund managers. It shows how much low-hanging fruit there is if you can react to news faster than the retail crowd."

content.text: The "Saying-is-Believing" Effect

Imagine you are a junior analyst on a busy M&A desk. Your Managing Director (MD) is absolutely desperate to get a deal over the line with a flashy tech startup. You look at the numbers, and they look... well, like a bin fire. The valuation is sky-high, the churn rate is terrifying, and the path to profitability is more of a scenic detour.

But you know how the game is played. You do not want to be the party pooper. So, when drafting the investment committee memo, you "tune" your message. You soften the risks, dress up the churn as "temporary market friction", and paint a beautiful picture of "synergistic growth". You pitch it beautifully.

Here is the scary part: three weeks later, you are not just pretending anymore. You genuinely believe it is a brilliant deal. You have forgotten your own initial scepticism. This is not just you being a corporate sellout; it is a well-documented psychological phenomenon known as the "Saying-is-Believing" (SIB) effect, driven by Audience Tuning.
How Your Brain Rewrites the Script

First identified by psychologists E. Tory Higgins and William S. Rholes in 1978, the Saying-is-Believing effect occurs when we adjust our communication to match the attitudes of our audience. In psychology, this is called "audience tuning".

Crucially, this tuning does not just change what we say—it changes what we remember. When we tailor a message to suit someone else's views, our brain works hard to build a "shared reality" with them. To maintain internal consistency and avoid cognitive dissonance, our memory of the original, objective facts is quietly overwritten by the biased version we just served up.

Interestingly, research shows this effect is strongest when we communicate with people we trust or want to build a relationship with (like a boss or a key client). If we are pitching to an "out-group" or someone we do not respect, we might still spin the story out of politeness, but our brain keeps the receipts and does not rewrite our actual memory.
The Danger in the City
In finance, this is where bad deals and disastrous investment decisions are born. It creates a dangerous feedback loop:

items: The Senior Signal: An MD or Portfolio Manager drops a hint about a stock or acquisition they like.
The Tuned Analysis: The team, wanting to please, writes a research note or model that highlights the positives and downplays the negatives.
The Self-Indoctrination: Because of the SIB effect, the analysts who wrote the biased report actually convince themselves that the stock is a screaming buy.
The Echo Chamber: The senior team reads the "objective" report, feels validated, and pulls the trigger on a terrible trade.

content.text: How to Use This at Work
If you want to keep your analytical edge (and your career) intact, you need to actively fight this bias:

items: Keep a "Cold-Hard-Facts" Journal: Before you write a single slide for a client pitch or an internal memo, write down your raw, unvarnished thoughts in a private notebook. When you find yourself getting swept up in the narrative later, go back and read your original assessment.

Hide Your Cards (for Managers): If you run a team, do not tell them your thesis before they do the work. If you say, "I think this logistics company is a great short play," you have just triggered audience tuning. Ask for their independent view first.

Appoint a "Devil's Advocate": If a team has spent weeks pitching a deal to a client, they are psychologically incapable of seeing the flaws anymore. Bring in a fresh pair of eyes who has not been involved in the "tuning" process to red-team the proposal.

content.text: One Line to Remember
Don't get high on your own supply: when you spin a story to please your audience, your brain rewrites its own memory to believe the spin.
